sections.subtitle: Gender & Number Agreement
sections.content:
📋 Adjectives MUST Match Nouns

Most -o adjectives:
• Masculine → -o
  → alto (tall)
• Feminine → -a
  → alta
• Masc. plural → -os
  → altos
• Fem. plural → -as
  → altas

✅ Adjectives ending in -e or consonants:
• Same for both genders
  → grande, fácil
• Add -s or -es for plural
  → grandes, fáciles

⚠️ Nationality adjectives (consonant ending):
• Add -a for feminine
  → español/española
  → inglés/inglesa

sections.subtitle: Position of Adjectives
sections.content:
📍 Where Adjectives Go

Most descriptive adjectives → AFTER noun:
• el coche rojo (the red car)
• la casa grande (the big house)
• el libro interesante (the interesting book)

Always BEFORE noun:
• Quantity → muchos libros
• Demonstratives → este perro
• Possessives → mi casa

💡 Meaning changes with position:
• un hombre grande → a big man (size)
• un gran hombre → a great man (quality)

• un coche nuevo → a new car (brand new)
• un nuevo coche → a new car (different car)

sections.subtitle: Apocopation: Shortened Forms
sections.content:
✂️ Drop Final Vowel (before masc. singular)

Common shortened forms:
• bueno → buen
  → buen día (good day)
• malo → mal
  → mal tiempo (bad weather)
• grande → gran
  → gran libro (great book)
• primero → primer
  → primer lugar (first place)
• tercero → tercer
  → tercer piso (third floor)

⚠️ ONLY before masculine singular nouns!
• buena casa (good house) - no change
• buenos días (good days) - no change

sections.subtitle: Comparatives: More & Less
sections.content:
⚖️ Comparing Things

More than:
• más + adjective + que
  → más alto que (taller than)
  → más inteligente que (smarter than)

Less than:
• menos + adjective + que
  → menos caro que (less expensive than)

Equal comparison (as...as):
• tan + adjective + como
  → tan rápido como (as fast as)
  → tan grande como (as big as)

⚠️ Irregular comparatives:
• bueno → mejor (better)
• malo → peor (worse)
• grande/viejo → mayor (older/bigger)
• pequeño/joven → menor (younger/smaller)

sections.subtitle: Superlatives: The Most/Least
sections.content:
🏆 The Most/Least

Pattern: article + más/menos + adjective + de

• el más alto de la clase
  → the tallest in the class
• la menos cara de todas
  → the least expensive of all
• los más inteligentes del grupo
  → the smartest in the group

⚠️ Irregular superlatives:
• el mejor (the best)
• el peor (the worst)

💯 Absolute superlative (-ísimo):
• altísimo → extremely tall
• facilísimo → extremely easy
• grandísimo → extremely big

sections.subtitle: Demonstrative & Possessive Adjectives
sections.content:
👉 Demonstratives (proximity)

Near (this/these):
• este/esta/estos/estas

Medium (that/those):
• ese/esa/esos/esas

Far (that/those - far):
• aquel/aquella/aquellos/aquellas

🤝 Possessives

• mi/mis → my
• tu/tus → your (informal)
• su/sus → his/her/your (formal)/their
• nuestro/nuestra/nuestros/nuestras → our
• vuestro/vuestra/vuestros/vuestras → your (plural, Spain)

✅ They agree in number with possessed item

questions.question: What is the feminine form of 'alto' (tall)?
questions.hint: Change the -o to -a for feminine adjectives.

questions.question: What is the plural of 'casa grande' (big house)?
questions.hint: Both the noun and adjective must be plural. Add -s to both words.

questions.question: What is the feminine form of 'español' (Spanish)?
questions.hint: Nationality adjectives ending in a consonant add -a for feminine.

questions.question: Where do most descriptive adjectives go in Spanish?
questions.hint: Unlike English, Spanish puts most descriptive adjectives after the noun: 'el coche rojo' (the red car).

questions.question: Which is correct for 'the red car'?
questions.hint: Descriptive adjectives go after the noun. Coche is masculine, so use 'rojo'.

questions.question: What is the apocopated form of 'bueno' before a masculine noun?
questions.hint: Drop the -o before masculine singular nouns. Example: buen día (good day).

questions.question: Which is correct for 'a good day'?
questions.hint: Bueno becomes 'buen' before masculine singular nouns and goes before the noun.

questions.question: What does 'grande' become before a singular noun?
questions.hint: Grande shortens to 'gran' before any singular noun (masculine or feminine).

questions.question: 'Un gran hombre' means...
questions.hint: When 'grande' becomes 'gran' and goes before the noun, it means 'great' (quality), not 'big' (size).

questions.question: How do you say 'taller than'?
questions.hint: Use más + adjective + que for 'more...than' comparisons.

questions.question: How do you say 'less expensive than'?
questions.hint: Use menos + adjective + que for 'less...than' comparisons.

questions.question: How do you say 'as fast as'?
questions.hint: Use tan + adjective + como for equality comparisons (as...as).

questions.question: What is the irregular comparative for 'good'?
questions.hint: Don't say 'más bueno'. Use the irregular form meaning 'better'.

questions.question: What is the irregular comparative for 'bad'?
questions.hint: Don't say 'más malo'. Use the irregular form meaning 'worse'.

questions.question: How do you say 'the tallest in the class'?

answers.text: el más alto de la clase
el alto más de la clase

questions.hint: Use el/la + más + adjective + de for superlatives (the most...).

questions.question: What does 'facilísimo' mean?
questions.hint: The -ísimo ending creates an absolute superlative meaning 'extremely' or 'very very'.

questions.question: Which demonstrative means 'this' (masculine)?
questions.hint: This is the nearest demonstrative, masculine singular form.

questions.question: Which demonstrative means 'that' (medium distance, feminine)?
questions.hint: This is the medium-distance demonstrative, feminine singular form.

questions.question: What is the possessive adjective for 'our' (feminine plural)?
questions.hint: 'Our' in Spanish changes form. Use the feminine plural form for feminine plural nouns.

questions.question: Which possessive is 'their/your (formal)' in Spanish?
questions.hint: This possessive is ambiguous - it can mean his, her, their, or your (formal). Context clarifies meaning.
